500 MILLION YEARS AGO
If you have ever
gently touched a pill
bug in your garden
and watched it instantly
curl into a tight
ball, you have seen
a defensive trick that
trilobites were using more
than five hundred million
years ago.
In the ancient seas,
survival was a brutal game.
By the Ordovician period,
giant sea scorpions prowled
the muddy bottom,
and shelled cephalopods
with sharp beaks hunted
in the water above.
To stay alive,
trilobites relied on one
of the most successful
defenses in the history
of animals: enrolment.
When danger came near,
a trilobite curled its
segmented body tightly
inward, tucking its soft
legs and delicate gills
safely inside.
Matching grooves and edges
along the head shield
and the tail plate
locked together with
surprising precision.
The animal became a
sealed ball of hard
mineral plates.
We know this worked,
and we know how
common it was,
because fossil trilobites
caught in a rolled-up
pose are found in
rocks all around the world.
Frozen in stone,
they are still guarding
their soft undersides.
For a very long
time, a trick like
this was a good
answer to the predators
of the day.
But evolution never stands
still.
Later, armored, jawed fish
arrived, and strong jaws
can crush a thin shell.
Many paleontologists think
the pressure sparked an
arms race.
Some trilobites grew forests
of sharp spikes.
Others developed
periscope-like eyes on
stalks, which may have
let them hide in
the mud and still
watch for danger.
Even the rolling itself
had limits.
A ball of armor
can protect the soft
parts, but it cannot
always protect the shell,
and a determined predator
could crack it.
That is the nature
of an arms race:
every defense invites a
stronger attack.
Every spine and every
stalk is a clue
about the hunters those
animals once feared.
So how did the
trilobites survive these
terrifying new hunters,
and what finally ended them?
Find out in our
full documentary on the
epic rise and fall
of the trilobites.
